doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Sonic Creed and art as a reflection of the world
summary: Monk Rowe praises the Hamilton concert video and reads about Sonic Creed; Harris says art matters because it captures what is happening in the world, as with Ellington, Hancock and Miles.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: Welcome, Mr. Harris. It’s a pleasure to see you.
Likewise. Thank you for having me, I’m looking forward to our conversation today. It’s always nice, under these circumstances, to communicate with people, whether it’s in- person or over Zoom.

Right. I mean normally I would — I give you a virtual handshake. I was lucky to see a preview of the concert that you filmed for Hamilton and I was very impressed first of all with the music, the interaction and the quality of it, so I appreciate and we appreciate you taking the time and effort to create the next best thing to being here. I wanted to read something from your website because I was saying to myself this video shows a very high standard when it comes to quality. This is what it said about Sonic Creed, a recent recording of yours. It says, “The album chronicles the story of people and their time on the planet, it’s a reflection of African-American life in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, and a sonic manifestation and creed of family, community and legacy.” So I think it’s safe to say that you set a very high bar for yourself and Blackout. Is that a fair statement?
Absolutely, and bigger than the idea that I set the bar, these people on the wall all around me, I’m surrounded by incredible artists —

You know every single day, from where I’m sitting at the piano or on the vibes, I’m writing and creating. I see a photo of Duke Ellington or whoever it is in my room and they remind me of the importance of staying focused on why art is important. Art is not important in our society because of the individual talent of an artist or an individual artist’s ego. Art is important because it’s a reflection of what’s happening in the world right now. The reason that Herbie Hancock back there and Miles Davis, all these people became so incredible wasn’t just their musicianship. It has more to do with the fact that they captured the essence of what was happening in the world at that time so that we gain a better understanding of how we got to the point that we’re at now.
